extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology; writers/students studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Close analytic guidance on using and identifying prolepses (anticipations) and related anachronies in narrative discourse, with distinctions, functions, textual marks, and examples (especially Proust). Useful for literary analysis and for writers thinking about temporal manipulation and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolepsis (anticipation) as narrative device
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of anticipation (prolepsis) in narrative: the narrator alludes to or recounts events that occur later in the diegetic story-world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person narration lends itself particularly well to anticipation because of its retrospective character, which authorizes the narrator to allude to the future and to his present situation; examples: Robinson Crusoe's early prophetic remarks, Rousseau's anticipatory indignation, and Proust's extensive use of prolepses in the Recherche. Prolepses can authenticate the narrative of the past and bring the narrating instance directly into play, thereby affecting voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs. external prolepses
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish internal prolepses (occurring within the temporal field of the first narrative) from external prolepses (occurring at a later point than the main temporal field).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal prolepses are limited by the last non-proleptic scene of the first narrative. External prolepses function most often as epilogues, continuing lines of action to their logical conclusion even if that conclusion happens later than the narrative's central day (examples in Proust: episodes after the Guermantes matinee considered external prolepses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Completing prolepses (filling future blanks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses that 'fill in ahead of time' a later blank in the narrative—anticipations that complete future ellipses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quick evocations of future years in school, the sequel of erotic relations, anticipatory sea-scene descriptions. Their function is to offset future ellipses or paralipses by supplying expected continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeating prolepses (advance notices/repeating)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses that lightly double or briefly allude to a narrative section that will be told in full later (an advance notice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are generally brief allusions—canonical formulae include 'we will see' or 'one will see later'—and play the role of advance notice, creating expectation in the reader's mind. Example paradigms: advance notice of the Montjouvain sacrilege scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative / generalizing (paradigmatic) prolepses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses that envisage in advance the whole series of occurrences that a first event will inaugurate, thereby functioning as paradigms for subsequent repetitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical for 'first time' scenes (first kiss, first dinner, first sight of the sea). They open a view onto later series and mark narrative impatience while also expressing nostalgia for 'primultimateness' (the inaugural lastness of the first time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice vs. advance mention
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate explicit advance notices (which anticipate and announce later events) from mere advance mentions (preparatory markers whose significance is only recognized later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance mention is an 'insignificant seed' at the moment of appearance and gains importance retrospectively (examples: early appearances or mentions of characters who only matter later). Advance notices are explicit anticipations that signal future importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterodiegetic vs. homodiegetic prolepses and interference risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider narratorial embedding: heterodiegetic prolepses (narrator outside the story) present no risk of duplication; homodiegetic prolepses (narrator as character) may cause interference or useless duplication between the first narrative and the proleptic section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among homodiegetic prolepses, further differentiate completing prolepses (fill blanks) from repeating prolepses (double later sections). Awareness of this risk informs decisions about where to place anticipations to avoid redundancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks and signals of prolepsis and their closure
rubrics_metrics.description: Textual markers that introduce prolepsis ('to anticipate for a moment', 'interrupting for a few moments', 'I take a leap of many years') and markers that signal return to the primary narrative ('to return to this first evening...', 'it is time to rejoin...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust frequently uses explicit verbal signs both to launch anticipations and to close them. Authors can choose explicitness to help readers follow complex temporal maneuvers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent: partial vs. complete prolepses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses may be partial (most common) or complete (rare): partial prolepses are often interrupted as abruptly as they begin; completeness would mean prolonging anticipation through to denouement or narrating moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes almost no clear examples of complete prolepses; most anticipations stop short, which affects how much closure they provide within the narrative timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolepses' effect on voice and 'omnitemporality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolepses that bring the narrating instance into play become data of voice: the narrator's simultaneous possession of the whole story produces a retrospective synthesis or 'omnitemporality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This retrospective omnitemporality (illustrated by Proust's narrator holding all threads simultaneously) fuses event and narrating instance, and affects tone and authority—anticipations in the narrator's present authenticate past narrative and are linked to voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader competence, detection of 'seeds', and authorial play (false snares)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how a reader's growing narrative competence affects detection of advance mentions and how authors exploit that competence with false advance mentions or 'snares' to mislead or surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skilled readers learn to identify 'seeds' and may outmaneuver authorial traps (detecting forthcoming events); authors can then deploy false snares or double-deceptions (advance mentions that are misleading) to produce subtle expectations and surprises—common in detective-story techniques and Proustian believability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-distance advance notices and architectural cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of long-reach anticipations to establish cohesion and justificatory links across widely separated parts of a work, reducing the impression of adventitious or gratuitous episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proust valued cohesiveness and used long-distance advance notices to provide provisional justification for distant episodes (examples: repeated anticipations that suggest later correspondences). This is useful in multi-volume works where separated publication can disguise planned symmetries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance anticipation of retrospective discovery (prolepsis of future memory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative moves where the narrator anticipates how he will later remember or be informed of a present incident (a prolepsis about a future recollection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This zigzag temporality (anticipating the memory of an event) speeds temporal seesawing (examples: 'I learned that a death had occurred that day which distressed me greatly, that of Bergotte'—elliptical shaping creates the effect). Such constructions complicate linear temporal consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-degree anachronies and toward achrony
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of complex layered anachronies—prolepses on analepses, analepses on prolepses, second- and third-degree effects—that can produce highly entangled temporal structures approaching achrony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples drawn from Proust and other texts show frequent second-degree prolepses and mixed anachronies at various narrative scales; analysts should be alert to these recursive and superimposed temporal operations when mapping narrative time.
